cards.front: How many bits are in an IPv4 address?
cards.back: 32 bits, organized as four octets of 8 bits each, usually written in dotted decimal.

cards.front: What is the dotted-decimal value of the binary octet 11000000?
What is the binary form of decimal 255?
An IPv4 address is divided into which two portions?
cards.back: The network portion (identifies the network) and the host portion (identifies the host on that network).

cards.front: What does a subnet mask do in an IPv4 address?
cards.back: It indicates which bits of the address are the network portion (1s) and which are the host portion (0s).

cards.front: What is the dotted-decimal subnet mask for prefix length /24?
What is the dotted-decimal subnet mask for prefix length /16?
What is the dotted-decimal subnet mask for prefix length /8?
How do you find the network address of a host given its IP and subnet mask?
cards.back: Perform a logical AND of the IP address and the subnet mask; the result is the network address.

cards.front: Given 192.168.10.33 with mask 255.255.255.0, what is the network address?
cards.back: 192.168.10.0 (the host octet 33 AND 0 = 0).

cards.front: What is a unicast IPv4 address?
cards.back: Identifies a single interface; a packet sent to it goes to exactly one host. The destination host bit is not all 1s.

cards.front: What is a broadcast IPv4 address?
cards.back: Identifies all hosts on a network; the host portion is all 1s. A packet sent to it reaches every host on the network.

cards.front: What is the directed broadcast address for network 192.168.10.0/24?
cards.back: 192.168.10.255 (host bits all set to 1).

cards.front: What is a multicast IPv4 address?
cards.back: Identifies a group of hosts; a packet is delivered to all members of that group. Uses the 224.0.0.0/4 range (Class D).

cards.front: Which IPv4 address range is reserved for private networks per RFC 1918 (Class A)?
Which IPv4 address range is reserved for private networks per RFC 1918 (Class B)?
Which IPv4 address range is reserved for private networks per RFC 1918 (Class C)?
What is the special-use IPv4 loopback range?
cards.back: 127.0.0.0/8 (127.0.0.0 to 127.255.255.255). Used to test the host's own TCP/IP stack.

cards.front: What is the special-use IPv4 link-local range?
cards.back: 169.254.0.0/16 (169.254.0.0 to 169.254.255.255). Used for automatic private addressing when no DHCP server is available.

cards.front: What is the TEST-NET IPv4 range used for documentation?
What is the default subnet mask of a Class A address?
What is the default subnet mask of a Class B address?
What is the default subnet mask of a Class C address?
What are the IPv4 address ranges for Classes A, B, C, D, and E?
What is a broadcast domain?
cards.back: The group of devices that receive a broadcast frame sent by any one of them. Routers do not forward broadcasts, so each router interface edge the a broadcast domain.

cards.front: What device breaks up broadcast domains?
cards.back: A router. Hosts on different router interfaces are in different broadcast domains.

cards.front: What device breaks up collision domains but not broadcast domains?
cards.back: A switch. Each switch port is its own collision domain, but the switch forwards broadcasts to all ports in the same broadcast domain.

cards.front: Give one reason to segment a network into smaller subnets.
cards.back: To reduce broadcast traffic and improve performance and security by limiting the size of broadcast domains.

cards.front: How do you compute the number of subnets created when borrowing n bits?
How do you compute the number of usable hosts in a subnet with h host bits?
cards.back: 2^h - 2 (subtract the network and broadcast addresses).

cards.front: Using the magic number method, what is the block size (magic number) for mask 255.255.255.192?
Using the magic number method, what is the block size for mask 255.255.255.224?
Using the magic number method, what is the block size for mask 255.255.255.240?
Using the magic number method, what is the block size for mask 255.255.255.248?
How many usable hosts are in a /24 subnet?
How many usable hosts are in a /25 subnet?
How many usable hosts are in a /26 subnet?
How many usable hosts are in a /27 subnet?
How many usable hosts are in a /28 subnet?
How many usable hosts are in a /29 subnet?
How many usable hosts are in a /30 subnet?
cards.back: 2 (2^2 - 2). Used for point-to-point links.

cards.front: What is the subnet mask for a /25 prefix?
What is the subnet mask for a /26 prefix?
What is the subnet mask for a /27 prefix?
What is the subnet mask for a /28 prefix?
What is the subnet mask for a /29 prefix?
What is the subnet mask for a /30 prefix?
Subnet 192.168.1.0/26. What are the subnet addresses?
cards.back: 192.168.1.0, .64, .128, .192. The magic number is 64, so subnets increment by 64.

cards.front: For subnet 192.168.1.64/26, what are the usable host addresses?
Subnet 172.16.0.0/16 into /24 subnets. How many subnets result?
cards.back: 256 (2^8, borrowing 8 bits).

cards.front: Subnet 172.16.0.0/16 into /24 subnets. What is the first usable subnet address?
cards.back: 172.16.0.0 (subnets increment by 1 in the third octet: .0, .1, .2 ... .255).

cards.front: Subnet 10.0.0.0/8 into /16 subnets. How many subnets result?
cards.back: 256 (2^8, borrowing 8 bits in the second octet).

cards.front: You need 30 usable hosts per subnet in a /24 network. What prefix length gives enough hosts with the least waste?
cards.back: /27 (gives 30 usable hosts exactly, 2^5 - 2).

cards.front: You need 50 usable hosts per subnet. What prefix length satisfies this with least waste?
cards.back: /26 (gives 62 usable hosts, 2^6 - 2).

cards.front: You need 8 subnets from a /24. How many bits must you borrow and what is the new mask?
cards.back: Borrow 3 bits (2^3 = 8), giving prefix /27, mask 255.255.255.224.

cards.front: What is VLSM?
cards.back: Variable-Length Subnet Masking: subnetting a network into subnets of different sizes, each with a mask that matches the number of hosts it needs, minimizing wasted addresses.

cards.front: When using VLSM, which subnets should you allocate first?
cards.back: The largest subnets (those needing the most hosts) first, so address space is used efficiently.

cards.front: What is a structured IP addressing design?
cards.back: A hierarchical, planned allocation of address blocks (e.g., one block per location, one subnet per segment) that makes networks easier to manage, troubleshoot, and summarize.

cards.front: Why should subnetting border a consistent, structured plan rather than random assignment?
cards.back: It simplifies route summarization, makes management and troubleshooting easier, and reduces errors.

cards.front: What is the primary reason to use private IPv4 addresses with NAT?
cards.back: To conserve public IPv4 address space; private addresses are reused inside networks and translated to public addresses at the edge.

cards.front: How many bits make up an IPv6 address? How is it written?
cards.back: 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons.

cards.front: In IPv6, what does omitting leading zeros mean in a group?
cards.back: Any leading zeros in a 4-digit group can be dropped. For example, 0db8 becomes db8.

cards.front: In IPv6, when can the double colon (::) be used?
cards.back: It replaces one contiguous run of all-zero groups and can only be used once per address, for the longest run of zeros.

cards.front: Expand the IPv6 address 2001:db8::1 to full form.
What is the compressed form of 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001?
What is the IPv6 loopback address?
cards.back: ::1 (all zeros except the last bit). Equivalent to IPv4 loopback 127.0.0.1.

cards.front: What is the IPv6 unspecified address?
cards.back: :: (all zeros). Used to indicate the absence of an address, e.g., as a source when a host has not yet obtained an address.

cards.front: What is the prefix for IPv6 global unicast addresses (GUA)?
cards.back: 2000::/3 (2000:: to 3fff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff).

cards.front: What is the prefix for IPv6 link-local addresses (LLA)?
cards.back: fe80::/10 (fe80:: to febf:...). Link-local addresses are automatically created and only work on the local link.

cards.front: What is the prefix for IPv6 unique local addresses (ULA)?
cards.back: fc00::/7 (fc00:: to fdff:...). They are like private IPv4 addresses, not routable on the public internet.

cards.front: What is the prefix for IPv6 multicast addresses?
cards.back: ff00::/8 (starting with ff).

cards.front: What is an IPv6 anycast address?
cards.back: An address that is assigned to multiple interfaces, typically on different nodes; a packet is delivered to only one of them, usually the nearest. It uses the same format as a unicast address.

cards.front: What is the IPv6 multicast address for all-nodes on the local link?
What is the IPv6 multicast address for all-routers on the local link?
What is the IPv6 multicast address used by OSPFv3 routers?
cards.back: ff02::5 (all OSPF routers).

cards.front: What is the IPv6 multicast address used by RIPng routers?
cards.back: ff02::9 (all RIPng routers).

cards.front: What is the IPv6 multicast address used by EIGRP routers?
cards.back: ff02::a (all EIGRP routers).

cards.front: What is the IPv6 solicited-node multicast address format and prefix?
cards.back: ff02::1:ff00:0/104. It is formed from the last 24 bits of a unicast address appended to ff02::1:ff00:0.

cards.front: Why does IPv6 use solicited-node multicast instead of broadcast?
cards.back: IPv6 has no broadcast. Solicited-node multicast is used by Neighbor Discovery to resolve addresses efficiently without waking all hosts on the link.

cards.front: What are the three strategies for IPv4-to-IPv6 coexistence?
cards.back: Dual stack (run both IPv4 and IPv6), tunneling (encapsulate IPv6 packets inside IPv4), and translation (convert between IPv4 and IPv6).

cards.front: What does dual stack mean?
cards.back: A device runs IPv4 and IPv6 at the same time, so it can communicate over either protocol.

cards.front: What does IPv6 tunneling do?
cards.back: It encapsulates an IPv6 packet inside an IPv4 packet so it can travel across an IPv4-only network.

cards.front: Which IPv6 address type is automatically created on every interface and never routed off the link?
cards.back: Link-local (fe80::/10).

cards.front: What command enables IPv6 unicast routing on a Cisco IOS router?
cards.back: ipv6 unicast-routing

cards.front: What is the Cisco IOS command to assign a static IPv6 global unicast address to an interface?
cards.back: ipv6 address 2001:db8::1/64 (in interface configuration mode).

cards.front: What is the Cisco IOS command to add an IPv6 link-local address to an interface?
cards.back: ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local

cards.front: What is the Windows netsh command to statically configure an IPv6 address?
cards.back: netsh interface ipv6 set address <interface> <address>

cards.front: What are the two methods by which an IPv6 host dynamically obtains a global unicast address?
cards.back: SLAAC and DHCPv6. SLAAC is the default; DHCPv6 can be stateless or stateful.

cards.front: How does SLAAC obtain an IPv6 address?
cards.back: Hosts send Router Solicitation (RS) messages; routers reply with Router Advertisement (RA) messages that carry the prefix, and the host builds its address from the prefix plus its interface ID.

cards.front: What is the difference between SLAAC and SLAAC + stateless DHCPv6?
cards.back: SLAAC provides prefix and default gateway only; adding stateless DHCPv6 lets hosts also get other settings like DNS server addresses, but not an address.

cards.front: What does stateful DHCPv6 provide?
cards.back: It assigns the IPv6 address and all configuration parameters (like DNS) to hosts, similar to stateful DHCPv4.

cards.front: What are the two ways a host can generate the interface ID (host portion) of an IPv6 address?
cards.back: EUI-64 (derived from the MAC address) or a randomly generated 64-bit interface ID for privacy.

cards.front: How is EUI-64 created from a MAC address?
cards.back: Split the 48-bit MAC in half, insert FFFE in the middle, and flip the universal/local (U/L) bit to 1. Example: MAC 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E becomes 021A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E.

cards.front: Why do modern hosts use a random interface ID instead of EUI-64?
cards.back: Privacy: EUI-64 is derived from the fixed MAC address, which lets others track the device across networks. Random IDs avoid this.

cards.front: How does a host dynamically create its IPv6 link-local address?
cards.back: Automatically, using the fe80::/10 prefix and an interface ID (EUI-64 or random), without needing a router.

cards.front: What Cisco IOS command shows the IPv6 addresses on all interfaces?
cards.back: show ipv6 interface brief

cards.front: What Cisco IOS command shows details and status of a single interface's IPv6 settings?
cards.back: show ipv6 interface <interface>

cards.front: How many /64 subnets can be created from a /48 prefix?
cards.back: 65536 (2^16, because 64 - 48 = 16 subnet bits).

cards.front: What is the standard prefix length for an IPv6 subnet on a LAN segment?
What is the Subnet ID in IPv6?
cards.back: The bits between the global routing prefix and the interface ID that let an organization create many subnets from one allocated prefix. E.g., a /48 can be subdivided into /64 subnets using the Subnet ID.

cards.front: If an ISP assigns a site 2001:db8:acad::/48, how do you create a /64 subnet for the first LAN?
cards.back: Use the next 16 bits as the Subnet ID, e.g., 2001:db8:acad:1::/64, :2::/64, and so on.

cards.front: What is the IPv6 prefix length for a link-local address?
What is the difference between TCP and UDP?
cards.back: TCP is connection-oriented, reliable, and ordered, with acknowledgments and retransmission. UDP is connectionless, best-effort, low-overhead, and does not guarantee delivery or ordering.

cards.front: Which transport protocol would you use for a video stream where losing a few packets is acceptable but delay is not?
cards.back: UDP, because it has low overhead and no retransmission delays.

cards.front: Which transport protocol would you use for a file download that must be complete and error-free?
cards.back: TCP, because it provides reliability, sequencing, and retransmission.

cards.front: What well-known port does HTTP use?
What well-known port does HTTPS use?
What well-known port does DNS use?
cards.back: 53 (UDP for queries, TCP for zone transfers).

cards.front: What well-known ports does DHCP use?
cards.back: 67 (server) and 68 (client).

cards.front: What well-known port does Telnet use?
cards.back: 23 (TCP, unencrypted).

cards.front: What well-known port does SSH use?
cards.back: 22 (TCP, encrypted).

cards.front: What well-known ports does FTP use?
cards.back: 20 (data) and 21 (control), both TCP.

cards.front: What well-known port does TFTP use?
What well-known port does SNMP use?
What well-known port does SMTP use?
What well-known port does POP3 use?
What well-known port does IMAP use?
Which protocols are used to send and receive email respectively?
cards.back: SMTP (25) sends/transfers; POP3 (110) or IMAP (143) receive. SMTP is often also on 587 for submission.

cards.front: What is the purpose of QoS (Quality of Service) for voice and video?
cards.back: It prioritizes delay-sensitive traffic, such as voice and video, over other traffic to keep latency and jitter low.

cards.front: A PC's IP address, subnet mask, and default gateway are all correct, but it cannot reach a remote server. What is the most likely single point to check first?
cards.back: Whether the default gateway is reachable and correctly configured; if the gateway is wrong, the host cannot route off the local subnet.

cards.front: What does the ping command do?
cards.back: It sends ICMP Echo Request messages to a destination and waits for Echo Replies to verify connectivity and measure round-trip time.

cards.front: What does an extended ping on Cisco allow you to do that a normal ping does not?
cards.back: It lets you set options interactively, such as source interface, packet size, repeat count, and timeout.

cards.front: What is the difference between traceroute (Cisco/Linux) and tracert (Windows)?
cards.back: They do the same job, show the route a packet takes hop by hop. Cisco/Linux use traceroute; Windows uses tracert.

cards.front: What does traceroute/tracert report at each hop?
cards.back: The IP address (or hostname) of each router along the path and the round-trip time to it, using ICMP (Windows) or UDP (Cisco/Linux) packets with increasing TTLs.

cards.front: What is an extended traceroute on Cisco?
cards.back: A traceroute where you interactively set options such as the source IP, timeout, and maximum hops.

cards.front: Why are documentation baselines useful for troubleshooting?
cards.back: A baseline records normal network performance so abnormal behavior can be detected and measured against a known-good state.

cards.front: What does the Windows command ipconfig /all display?
cards.back: Full TCP/IP configuration of each interface, including IP, mask, default gateway, DNS servers, MAC address, and DHCP lease info.

cards.front: What does the Linux/Unix ifconfig command display?
cards.back: Configured network interfaces and their IPv4 addresses, masks, flags, and MAC addresses. (Legacy; ip addr is newer.)

cards.front: What does the Linux command ip addr show?
cards.back: Detailed address information for all interfaces, including both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, masks, and flags.

cards.front: What does the arp -a command do?
cards.back: Shows the ARP cache, mapping IPv4 addresses to MAC addresses on the local network.

cards.front: What does the Cisco command show cdp neighbors display?
cards.back: A list of directly connected Cisco neighbor devices discovered via CDP, including device ID, local interface, and platform.

cards.front: What does the Cisco command show ip interface brief display?
cards.back: A summary of all interfaces with their IP address, status, protocol status, and whether they are up.

cards.front: What does the Cisco command show version display?
cards.back: Cisco IOS version, system uptime, hardware/platform information, and the amount of RAM and flash.

cards.front: What does the Cisco command show ip route display?
cards.back: The IPv4 routing table, showing directly connected and learned routes and their next hops.

cards.front: What does the Cisco command show interfaces display?
cards.back: Detailed status, statistics, and configuration of all interfaces, including errors, collisions, and line protocol state.

cards.front: What does the Cisco command show running-config display?
cards.back: The current running configuration in RAM, including all configured commands.

cards.front: What is the purpose of the debug command on Cisco IOS?
cards.back: It provides real-time, detailed diagnostic output about events such as packets being processed. It can heavily load the device.

cards.front: Why must you use terminal monitor when using debug over a remote connection?
cards.back: Debug messages are shown on the console by default; terminal monitor redirects them to your remote (VTY) session so you can see them.

cards.front: What command turns off all debugging on a Cisco device?
cards.back: undebug all (or no debug all).

cards.front: What is the top-down troubleshooting method?
cards.back: Start at the application layer and work down through the OSI layers to the physical. Best when the problem is likely in software or the application.

cards.front: What is the bottom-up troubleshooting method?
cards.back: Start at the physical layer and work up. Best when the problem is likely hardware or physical, such as a bad cable.

cards.front: What is the divide-and-conquer troubleshooting method?
cards.back: Start at a middle layer (often the network layer) and test, then move up or down based on the result to isolate the fault.

cards.front: What should you do if you cannot resolve a problem within your ability or access?
cards.back: Escalate it to a higher-level support team or engineer, documenting what you found and tried.

cards.front: A device has a duplex mismatch (one side full-duplex, the other half-duplex). What symptom would you expect?
cards.back: High numbers of late collisions and CRC/alignment errors on the half-duplex side, plus slow throughput.

cards.front: A host is assigned an IP address of 169.254.x.x. What does this indicate?
cards.back: The host could not reach a DHCP server and assigned itself a link-local APIPA address, so it has no valid network connectivity.

cards.front: Two PCs on the same VLAN cannot ping each other. The switch ports are up. What is a likely addressing cause?
cards.back: They are in different subnets (wrong IP/mask), so they are in different broadcast domains and cannot communicate directly without a router.

cards.front: A host can ping its own IP and other local hosts but not anything off the local network. What is the likely cause?
cards.back: The default gateway is missing, wrong, or down; the host cannot route packets off the local subnet.

cards.front: A host can reach a server by IP address but not by hostname. What service is failing?
cards.back: DNS resolution. The host cannot translate the name to an IP, so check the DNS server setting and reachability.

cards.front: What is the role of the default gateway on a host?
cards.back: It is the IP address of the router interface on the host's subnet; the host sends all packets destined for other networks to it.

cards.front: Which tool is used to examine packets in detail, such as seeing TCP handshake or application-layer data?
cards.back: Wireshark, a protocol analyzer (packet sniffer).
